title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
authors: Meriem Terki, Nouhaila Innan, Minghao Shao, Muhammad Kashif, Alberto Marchisio, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
summary: This paper introduces QTestBench, a novel framework to rigorously evaluate the quality of test suites generated by Large Language Models for quantum code. It moves beyond simple solution checking by measuring how well the generated tests can distinguish correct quantum implementations from faulty ones. The framework provides a reproducible benchmark, highlighting that while LLMs can write executable tests, their ability to detect bugs remains a significant challenge.
main_problem: Existing quantum benchmarks only assess if LLMs generate correct quantum solutions, failing to measure if the generated *tests* can reliably distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones.
main_result: The best LLM generator achieved a test quality of 0.71 on QHack, demonstrating that mere executability overstates the true test quality.
method: The authors introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites by comparing test verdicts against an independent benchmark checker across three validation cohorts.
model_or_system: The work focuses on quantum code generation for quantum circuits, tested using established platforms like PennyLane QHack and Qiskit HumanEval tasks.
key_observables: Test Quality Score (TQS), Executability Score (ES), Correctness Score (CS), and Bug-Detection Score (BDS).
important_parameters: The evaluation involves syntactic, semantic, and behavioral test types, and uses oracle-verified synthetic mutants when natural faulty solutions are scarce.
main_assumptions: The framework explicitly treats the generated tests as non-ground truth, relying instead on independent benchmark checkers as the oracle.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QTestBench pipeline, showing the comparison of test verdicts against checker labels, and tables summarize mean performance scores across different LLMs on QHack and Qiskit tasks.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem gap, details the QTestBench framework (two-stage pipeline), presents the metrics (ES, CS, BDS, TQS, CQ), benchmarks several LLMs on QHack and Qiskit, and discusses the implications of the results.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, rigorous evaluation methodology for assessing the trustworthiness of AI-generated quantum verification code, which is vital for advancing quantum software development.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Illustrative generated-test assertions for the Coffee Conundrum challenge (Table I). Each snippet shows the discriminating checks; harness boilerplate is omitted.

Fig. 2: QTestBench pipeline. Inputs: task description, official cases, and benchmark checker (oracle). Stage 1 generates syntactic, semantic, and behavioral pytest modules (one LLM call per type, temperature 0.8, no repair loop). Stage 2 builds a solution cohort, labels probes with the oracle, executes generated tests via runtime solution injection, and reports the metrics in Section III-C under Configuration A (trusted correct only), Configuration B (checker-labeled LLM cohort), and Configuration C (synthetic incorrect calibration; Section III-D).
Fig. 3: Core assertion patterns for the three generated test types (Table II), exemplified on the Rainy Days challenge.
Fig. 4: Three case studies on challenges other than the motivational example, connecting QTestBench metrics to concrete oracle vs. test outcomes.
